title: How to Speed Up Alcohol Metabolism: What Works and What's a Myth
excerpt: Can you make your body process alcohol faster? Mostly no. Why your liver works at a fixed pace, what helps a little (food, pacing, sleep), which sobering tricks are myths, and what DHM research really shows.
metaDescription: Can you speed up alcohol metabolism? Mostly no. Why your liver clears alcohol at a fixed rate, what helps a little, and which sober-up tricks are myths.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** you mostly can't speed up alcohol metabolism. Your liver breaks alcohol down at a fairly fixed rate, and almost nothing you can do in the moment changes that rate in a way that matters. Coffee, cold showers, a run, a sauna, or a big glass of water can change how you *feel*, but they do not lower your blood alcohol any faster. The one thing with reasonable research behind it is food, and even that only nudges the numbers. Time is what sobers you up.

That's not the answer most people want, but it's the one that keeps you safe. This guide explains why the rate is so fixed, which small things actually help at the margins, which popular tricks are myths, and what the research on DHM and alcohol enzymes really shows.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Never drive or operate machinery** after drinking based on how you feel or on any trick in this article. **Call 911 if someone** cannot be woken, is breathing slowly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregularly, has blue or pale skin, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while confused or drowsy. Do not leave a very drunk person alone to "sleep it off." If you drink heavily most days or have liver disease, talk to your doctor before taking any supplement, including DHM.

## Why You Can't Really Speed It Up: Zero-Order Kinetics in Plain Words

Most drugs leave your body in a way that scales with how much is there. The more you have in your blood, the faster your body clears it. Pharmacologists call that "first-order" elimination.

Alcohol is different. At the levels you reach from normal social drinking, it follows what's called **zero-order kinetics**. In plain terms, your liver clears a roughly fixed *amount* of alcohol per hour, no matter how much is waiting in line. It's like a checkout lane with one cashier working at a steady pace: a longer queue doesn't make the cashier scan faster.

The reason is enzyme capacity. The main enzyme that breaks down alcohol, **alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)**, gets saturated at fairly low blood alcohol levels. Once it's working at full speed, adding more alcohol just makes the queue longer. The Swedish scientist Erik Widmark described this straight-line fall in blood alcohol in the 1930s, and it's still the basis for how forensic scientists estimate blood alcohol today.

For more detail on absorption, distribution, and elimination, see our deep dive on [alcohol pharmacokinetics](/never-hungover/alcohol-pharmacokinetics-advanced-absorption-science-2025).

### The two-step chemistry

Your liver handles alcohol in two main steps:

1. **Alcohol to acetaldehyde.** ADH converts ethanol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that contributes to flushing, nausea, and some of the misery of drinking.
2. **Acetaldehyde to acetate.** A second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH)**, mainly a form called ALDH2, converts acetaldehyde into acetate, which is harmless and eventually becomes carbon dioxide and water.

A backup system in the liver, called the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (it relies on an enzyme called CYP2E1), handles a share of the load, especially at higher blood alcohol levels and in people who drink heavily on a regular basis.

Both main steps depend on a helper molecule called NAD+. The supply of NAD+ is one of the reasons the whole process has a speed limit. You can't simply eat or drink your way to more of it in the moment.

### How fast is "fixed"?

Forensic research summarized by toxicologist A. W. Jones (including a large review in *Forensic Science International*, 2010) puts the typical fall in blood alcohol at around **0.015 percent per hour** in moderate drinkers, with a normal range of roughly 0.010 to 0.025 percent per hour. That works out to something like one standard drink per hour for many adults, though body size, sex, genetics, liver health, and drinking history all shift it.

A standard drink in the US is about 14 grams of pure alcohol: a 12-ounce regular beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits. Many real-world drinks are bigger than that. A large pour of wine or a strong cocktail can count as two.

Here's what the math looks like. If you reach a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent (the legal driving limit in most of the US), it would take an average person about five hours to get back to zero at 0.015 percent per hour. At 0.15 percent, it's closer to ten hours. That's why people who drank late into the night can still be over the legal limit the next morning.

### Why the clock starts later than you think

There's one more catch. Your blood alcohol keeps *rising* for a while after your last drink as alcohol in your stomach and small intestine gets absorbed. Peak levels often arrive 30 to 90 minutes after you stop, depending on what you ate and how fast you drank. So "I stopped an hour ago" doesn't mean you're an hour into sobering up.

## What Actually Helps at the Margins

None of these turn a five-hour wait into a one-hour wait. They're worth knowing because they can help a little, and because several of them also make the night safer and the morning easier.

### 1. Eat a real meal, ideally before you start

This is the best-supported item on the list. Food in your stomach does two useful things:

- **It slows absorption.** Food keeps alcohol in the stomach longer before it moves to the small intestine, where most absorption happens. That means a lower, later peak blood alcohol level. Lower peaks matter for safety and for how impaired you get.
- **It seems to speed up elimination a bit.** In controlled studies, people who ate a meal cleared alcohol faster than when they drank on an empty stomach. Work by Jones and Jönsson (*Journal of Forensic Sciences*, 1994) and by Ramchandani and colleagues (*Journal of Clinical Pharmacology*, 2001) found faster elimination rates after a meal, and the effect didn't depend much on whether the meal was mostly carbs, fat, or protein. Researchers think a meal increases blood flow to the liver and may help the liver regenerate the NAD+ it needs.

The honest framing: eating raises the speed limit modestly. It does not remove it. And eating *after* you're already drunk helps much less than eating before or while drinking, because much of the alcohol has already been absorbed.

### 2. Pace yourself and alternate with water

This doesn't speed up your liver at all. What it does is keep the queue shorter. If your liver clears about one drink an hour and you drink one drink an hour, your blood alcohol stays much lower than if you have four in the first hour.

Alternating each drink with a glass of water is the simplest pacing tool there is. It also helps with fluid loss, since alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Staying hydrated won't flush alcohol out (more on that below), but it can take the edge off a dry mouth, thirst, and some headache the next day.

### 3. Sleep, but safely

Sleeping doesn't make the liver work faster. It's simply the most comfortable way to let the hours go by. A few caveats:

- **Alcohol wrecks sleep quality.** It tends to knock you out quickly, then fragments sleep later in the night and suppresses REM sleep. That's part of why you can sleep eight hours and still feel awful. Our guide on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) covers this in detail.
- **Don't let a very drunk person sleep alone.** Blood alcohol can keep climbing after someone passes out. Lay them on their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit, and check on them. If they can't be woken or their breathing is slow or irregular, call 911.
- **You can wake up still impaired.** If you went to bed at a high level, do the math above before driving in the morning.

### 4. Don't add more alcohol (including "hair of the dog")

It sounds obvious, but a morning drink resets the queue. It may briefly dull hangover symptoms, partly by delaying the drop in blood alcohol, but it just pushes the reckoning later and adds more work for your liver.

### 5. Be honest about your own baseline

Some factors change your speed in ways you can't control in the moment:

- **Body size and composition.** Alcohol spreads through body water. Smaller people and people with less lean mass reach higher levels from the same drink.
- **Sex.** On average, women reach higher blood alcohol levels than men from the same amount, mostly because of differences in body water.
- **Genetics.** Common variants of the ADH and ALDH2 genes change how fast alcohol and acetaldehyde are processed. The ALDH2 variant common in people of East Asian descent causes acetaldehyde to build up, which shows up as facial flushing. See our [Asian flush guide](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive).
- **Drinking history.** People who drink heavily over a long period often clear alcohol faster, because the CYP2E1 backup system ramps up. That is not a benefit. It's a sign of a liver adapting to a heavy load, and it comes with higher risk of liver injury and harmful drug interactions.
- **Liver health and medications.** Liver disease slows clearance. Some medicines interact with alcohol or compete for the same enzymes.

## Myths That Don't Speed Up Alcohol Metabolism

These are the tricks people reach for most often when they want to "sober up fast." They share a common problem: they change how alert you feel without changing how much alcohol is in your blood.

### Myth: Coffee sobers you up

Caffeine is a stimulant. It can reduce sleepiness, which is one of the more obvious signs of being drunk. But it doesn't lower blood alcohol, and studies of people given alcohol with and without caffeine have generally found that caffeine doesn't restore reaction time, judgment, or coordination to sober levels.

The real risk is the gap between how you feel and how impaired you are. Researchers sometimes call this being "wide-awake drunk." Someone who feels alert after an espresso is more likely to think they can drive. That's also one of the main safety concerns with mixing energy drinks and alcohol.

### Myth: A cold shower will snap you out of it

A cold shower is a jolt to the nervous system. You'll feel more awake for a few minutes. Your blood alcohol won't change. For someone who is very drunk, a cold shower adds risks: slipping, falling, and a sudden drop in body temperature, which alcohol already makes harder to regulate.

### Myth: You can sweat it out

The idea is that a sauna, a hot bath, or a hard workout pushes alcohol out through your skin. In reality, more than 90 percent of alcohol is broken down by the liver. Only a small remainder leaves unchanged through breath, urine, and sweat. Sweating more doesn't change the liver's pace.

Exercising or sitting in a sauna while drunk is risky. Alcohol already causes fluid loss and impairs balance and temperature control. Add heat and exertion and you raise the chance of dehydration, fainting, falls, and strain on your heart rhythm. Save the workout for when you're sober.

### Myth: Drinking lots of water flushes it out

Water helps with thirst and dehydration. It doesn't wash alcohol out of your blood, because the kidneys remove only a small fraction of it. Drinking huge amounts of water quickly can also be dangerous in its own right, because it can drop the sodium level in your blood. Steady, normal amounts are the goal.

### Myth: Throwing up gets the alcohol out

Vomiting can only remove alcohol that's still sitting in your stomach. By the time most people throw up, much of what they drank has already been absorbed. It doesn't lower the alcohol in your blood. Never make someone vomit on purpose, and treat vomiting in a drowsy or confused person as a warning sign, because they can choke.

### Myth: Eating greasy food the morning after cures it

A big breakfast can make you feel better, and food is helpful *before* and *during* drinking. The morning after, though, the alcohol is either already gone or still being cleared at the liver's usual rate. A bacon sandwich won't speed that up. It may help with low blood sugar and nausea, which is a fine reason to eat.

### Myth: Fresh air, walking it off, or a nap will sober you up for driving

A walk might make you feel more alert, and a short nap might make you less groggy. Neither drops your blood alcohol meaningfully in an hour. If you're over the limit at 11 pm, you're very likely still over it at midnight, nap or no nap.

### Myth: Breath mints, mouthwash, or tricks fool a breathalyzer

They don't change your blood alcohol. Some mouthwashes contain alcohol and can actually raise a breath reading briefly. This doesn't make anyone safer to drive.

### What about fructose, vitamins, or IV drips?

- **Fructose and sugar.** Some older lab and clinical studies reported that large doses of fructose slightly increased alcohol elimination, but results have been inconsistent and the doses involved aren't practical. It isn't a reliable sobering tool.
- **B vitamins and electrolyte drinks.** These can help replace what alcohol depletes and may help you feel better the next day. They don't change the clearance rate.
- **IV hydration clinics.** These treat dehydration and sometimes nausea. They don't remove alcohol from your blood faster.

In a hospital, doctors treating severe alcohol poisoning focus on protecting breathing, blood sugar, and body temperature while the liver does its work. In rare, extreme cases, dialysis can be used to remove alcohol directly. The fact that the standard medical approach is mostly supportive care tells you how little anyone can speed up the process.

## How to Sober Up Fast: The Honest Version

If you searched for how to sober up fast or how to get alcohol out of your system, here is what actually works:

1. **Stop drinking now.** Every drink you skip is roughly an hour you don't have to wait.
2. **Eat something** if you haven't, especially if you're still early in the night.
3. **Drink water at a normal pace.**
4. **Arrange a safe ride home.** A rideshare, a sober friend, public transit, or a couch for the night. This is the step that actually protects you.
5. **Get some sleep, on your side, with someone checking on you** if you drank a lot.
6. **Do the math before driving in the morning.** If you're not sure, don't drive. A personal breathalyzer can give a rough reading, but consumer devices vary in accuracy, and feeling fine is not evidence that you are.

Then accept that the rest is time. Your liver is already working as fast as it can.

## DHM and Alcohol Enzymes: What the Research Shows (and Doesn't)

Since this is a site about DHM (dihydromyricetin, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, *Hovenia dulcis*), it's fair to ask whether it speeds up alcohol metabolism. Here's the honest picture.

### What's been studied

- **Brain effects in rats.** The study that put DHM on the map, by Shen and colleagues in *The Journal of Neuroscience* (2012), looked at how DHM affects GABA-A receptors in the brain. It found that DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal in rats. That's about how alcohol acts on the brain, not about how fast it's cleared.
- **Liver enzyme effects in mice.** Research from a University of Southern California group led by Silva and Liang (*Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, 2020) reported that DHM-treated mice given alcohol showed increased expression of the alcohol-processing enzymes ADH and ALDH, faster ethanol metabolism, and less liver fat buildup. That's interesting and is the main reason DHM is linked to alcohol metabolism.
- **Antioxidant and liver-protection work.** Several animal and lab studies suggest DHM may reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in liver cells exposed to alcohol.

### What hasn't been shown

- **There's no solid human evidence that DHM lowers your blood alcohol faster in a way that matters.** Mouse results often don't carry over to people, and the doses don't translate neatly.
- **DHM does not make you safe to drive.** Even if it nudged enzyme activity in humans, the zero-order speed limit described above would still apply. Nothing in the research supports using DHM to shorten the time before you drive.
- **Human hangover data is limited.** Most of what people report about DHM is about how they feel the next day, and controlled human trials are still sparse.

We go through the full evidence, study by study, in [DHM science explained](/never-hungover/dhm-science-explained) and in our honest review, [does DHM work?](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025)

### If you want to try it

The reasonable way to think about DHM is as a possible aid for how you feel the next day, not a sobering tool. If you want to try it, a single-ingredient option like [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) keeps things simple. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers typical amounts and timing. If you take prescription medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have liver disease, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## How Long Until You're Actually Sober?

People often mix up three different timelines:

- **Peak intoxication.** Usually 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink, longer after a large meal.
- **Back to zero blood alcohol.** Roughly the peak level divided by about 0.015 percent per hour, with plenty of variation from person to person. After a heavy night, that can mean late morning or even early afternoon.
- **Feeling normal again.** A hangover typically peaks around when blood alcohol hits zero and can last much of the following day. Our guide to [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) breaks this down.

Note that alcohol can show up on some tests long after you're sober. Breath and blood tests reflect current alcohol. Urine tests that look for alcohol breakdown products, like ethyl glucuronide, can detect drinking for a day or more afterward. Being sober and testing negative are not always the same thing.

## A Smarter Goal: Lower Peaks, Not Faster Clearance

Since you can't do much about the speed of clearance, the most useful thing you can control is how high your blood alcohol gets in the first place. A lower peak means less impairment, less time waiting, and usually a milder morning.

That comes down to a few habits:

- Eat a proper meal before you go out.
- Decide on a number of drinks in advance and count standard drinks honestly.
- Space drinks out, roughly one per hour, and alternate with water.
- Choose lower-strength drinks when you can.
- Plan your way home before you start.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers these strategies in more depth.

## When to Get Help

Alcohol poisoning is a medical emergency. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone:

- Can't be woken or responds only weakly
- Is breathing slowly or with long gaps between breaths
- Has blue-tinged, pale, or clammy skin
- Is vomiting while confused, drowsy, or semi-conscious
- Has a seizure
- Has a low body temperature

Don't wait for every sign to appear. Don't give coffee, a cold shower, or food as a fix. Keep them on their side, stay with them, and get help.

If you find yourself regularly looking for ways to sober up faster, or drinking more than you planned, it may be worth talking to a doctor. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is free, confidential, and open 24 hours a day.

## The Bottom Line

- Your liver clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate, about one standard drink an hour for many adults, and you can't meaningfully speed that up in the moment.
- Eating a meal before or while drinking is the best-supported way to lower your peak and modestly speed elimination.
- Pacing, water, and sleep help you feel better and keep the night safer, but they don't clear alcohol faster.
- Coffee, cold showers, sweating, vomiting, and fresh air are myths when it comes to lowering blood alcohol.
- DHM has interesting animal research on alcohol enzymes, but no good human evidence that it sobers you up faster. Never use it as a reason to drive.
- Time is the only thing that works. Plan your ride home accordingly.

**Related reading:** [how alcohol is metabolized, step by step](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you speed up alcohol metabolism?**

Not by much. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults (with wide individual variation), and that rate barely changes no matter what you do. Eating a meal while or before drinking is the one thing with decent research behind it for modestly faster clearance. Coffee, cold showers, exercise, and sweating do not meaningfully speed it up. Time is the only reliable way to sober up.

**Does coffee sober you up?**

No. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but it does not lower your blood alcohol level or speed up how fast your liver breaks alcohol down. Your reaction time, judgment, and coordination stay impaired. The danger is that feeling more awake can make people think they are fine to drive or keep drinking when they are not.

**Does sleeping help get alcohol out of your system faster?**

Sleep does not make your liver work faster, but it is a safe way to let the hours pass while your body does the work. The main caveat is safety: someone who has drunk a large amount should not be left alone to sleep it off, because blood alcohol can keep rising after they pass out. If someone cannot be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or is vomiting while drowsy, call 911.

**Does drinking water flush alcohol out of your system?**

No. Only a small fraction of alcohol leaves through urine, breath, and sweat. More than 90 percent is broken down by the liver, and drinking water does not change that rate. Water is still worth drinking because alcohol makes you lose fluid and alternating drinks with water slows your pace, but it does not clear alcohol faster.

**How long does it take for alcohol to leave your body?**

A common rule of thumb is about one standard drink per hour, with blood alcohol falling by roughly 0.015 percent per hour on average. Individual rates vary, and the clock starts after the alcohol is absorbed, not when you finish your last drink. After a heavy night, it can easily be the next morning or later before your blood alcohol is back to zero.

**Does DHM speed up alcohol metabolism?**

There is some animal research suggesting DHM may increase the activity of the liver enzymes that break down alcohol, but there is no solid human evidence that it lowers your blood alcohol level faster in any meaningful way. DHM should never be used as a reason to drive, to drink more, or to think you have sobered up sooner. People mostly take it for how they feel the next day, and even that evidence is limited.

**Can you sweat out alcohol by exercising or using a sauna?**

No. Sweat removes only a tiny amount of alcohol, and exercise does not meaningfully speed up the liver. Hard exercise or saunas while drunk add real risks, including dehydration, overheating, falls, and heart rhythm strain. Wait until you are sober.

**Does throwing up lower your blood alcohol?**

Only if there is still unabsorbed alcohol in your stomach, and by the time most people vomit, much of it has already been absorbed. Vomiting does not remove alcohol from your blood. Never make someone vomit on purpose. Vomiting while very drunk can lead to choking, which is a medical emergency.
